intro.html: How do you describe the way something looks? A room can be beautiful, fancy, rich, flashy or bare, and each word tells the reader whether you admire it or wince at it.

Beauty: aesthetic (to do with beauty), exquisite (delicate and fine), sublime (awe-inspiring). Rich and fancy: ornate, opulent. Showing off: ostentatious, flamboyant. Too much: gaudy, garish. Bare: austere.
Pay attention to tone. Ornate and opulent can be praise or a gentle complaint; ostentatious, gaudy and garish always criticize; flamboyant can be either, depending on whether you enjoy the show.

words.def: having to do with beauty or the enjoyment of beauty
words.ex: The bridge is useful, but its {aesthetic} appeal is what draws the photographers.
words.ctx: The engineers cared only whether the tower would stand; the architect worried about its {aesthetic} qualities, arguing for curves and colored glass that would make it beautiful.
words.etym: From Greek aisthetikos, “having to do with the senses, with perception.”
words.note: Aesthetic (about beauty) is not ascetic (living a strict, self-denying life). It is sometimes spelled esthetic.

mn.text: At the art show, Professor Edwin peers at each painting and asks, “Is that ick, or is that lovely?” He is judging its {aesthetic} value.

scene.alt: An old professor studies a painting on an easel through a magnifier while the nervous artist waits.

words.ex: The tiny ship inside the bottle was {exquisite}, right down to its silk sails.
words.ctx: Every detail of the music box was {exquisite}: the dancer’s painted face was no bigger than a grain of rice, yet you could see her smile.
words.etym: From Latin exquisitus, “sought out, choice,” from exquirere: ex- (out) + quaerere (to seek).

mn.text: Lin searched every shop in the city for the finest teacup, and the one she finally found, painted with tiny gold birds, is {exquisite}.

scene.alt: A woman holds up a delicate, sparkling teacup she has finally found, gazing at it with delight.

words.def: so grand or beautiful that it fills one with awe
words.ex: From the mountaintop, the sunrise over the valley was {sublime}.
words.ctx: Critics expected a pleasant concert, but the performance was {sublime}; when the last note faded, the audience sat in stunned silence before bursting into applause.

mn.cue: SUB-LIME: climb up HIGH for a GRAND view
mn.text: After climbing all morning, Jamal reaches the summit and watches the sun rise over a sea of clouds; the view is so grand he cannot speak. It is {sublime}.

scene.alt: A hiker raises his arms in awe at the summit as the sun rises over a sea of clouds.

words.ex: The old theater had an {ornate} ceiling painted gold and carved with vines and birds.
words.ctx: Grandma’s clock was {ornate}, with gilded vines curling around its face and tiny brass birds on top; the new clock beside it was a plain white circle.
words.etym: From Latin ornatus, “decorated,” from ornare (to adorn, to furnish). Ornament comes from the same root.

mn.text: The king’s throne is covered in ornaments: golden curls, jewels, carved lions and a velvet cushion. It is {ornate}.

scene.alt: A proud king points to his golden, jewel-covered throne room.

words.ex: The hotel lobby was {opulent}, with marble floors and crystal chandeliers.
words.ctx: After years in a tiny apartment, the family found the mansion almost too {opulent}: velvet curtains, golden faucets and a fountain in the front hall.
words.etym: From Latin opulentus, “wealthy,” from ops (wealth, resources).

mn.text: The pampered cat naps on a velvet pillow, eats from a golden bowl and wears a tiny jeweled crown; visitors say “Ooh!” Its life is {opulent}.

scene.alt: A cat in a tiny crown lounges on a velvet pillow beside a golden bowl and a treasure chest.

words.def: showy in order to impress others
words.ex: He drove an {ostentatious} gold car with his name painted on both doors.
words.ctx: Most guests wore simple clothes to the picnic, but Mr. Hale arrived looking {ostentatious}, in a white suit and three diamond rings, mentioning his yacht every five minutes.
words.etym: From ostentation, from Latin ostentare, “to show off,” related to ostendere (to show).

mn.cue: os-TENT-atious: a GOLD TENT to show off
mn.text: At the campground, Victor pitches a golden tent with a flag and a sign bearing his name, just so everyone will look; that showing off is {ostentatious}.

scene.alt: A show-off in sunglasses and a top hat poses proudly beside his golden tent at a campsite.

words.def: bold, colorful and showy in a way that draws attention
words.ex: The {flamboyant} magician wore a purple cape covered in silver stars.
words.ctx: Her quiet sister dressed in gray, but Rosa was {flamboyant}: she wore a feathered hat, sang on the bus and greeted everyone with a sweeping bow.
words.etym: From French flamboyant, “flaming,” from flamboyer (to blaze).

mn.text: Jonah twirls into the party in a red-and-orange cape that ripples like fire, then takes a sweeping bow; he is {flamboyant}.

scene.alt: A teen in a flame-colored cape twirls on a stage in the spotlight.

words.def: too bright or showy in a tasteless way
words.ex: The {gaudy} sweater had blinking lights, sequins and a plastic snowman sewn on the front.
words.ctx: The old diner had a simple charm until the new owner covered it in {gaudy} decorations: neon flamingos, flashing arrows and gold plastic palm trees.
words.etym: From gaud, an old word for a showy trinket.

mn.text: Uncle Marcus wears a neon-pink tie, sparkly sunglasses, a party hat and six necklaces to the family picnic; everyone gawks, because his outfit is {gaudy}.

scene.alt: A man in a pink tie, party hat, sunglasses and jewelry poses while two teens stare in shock.

words.def: so bright and showy that it is unpleasant
words.ex: The {garish} orange paint made the little cottage look like a traffic cone.
words.ctx: The soft candlelight of the café was replaced by {garish} neon signs that buzzed and flashed so brightly that diners squinted at their plates.

mn.text: Pip paints the doghouse lime green, hot pink and orange all at once; the colors glare so hard that Grandpa puts on sunglasses. They are {garish}.

scene.alt: A boy proudly shows off a doghouse painted in glaring colors while his grandfather shields his eyes.

words.def: plain and without decoration; also, stern and strict
words.ex: The cabin was {austere}: a cot, a wooden chair and a single lamp.
words.ctx: Unlike his flashy brother, the old judge lived an {austere} life, eating simple meals, wearing the same gray coat for years and spending almost nothing on himself.
words.etym: From Latin austerus, from Greek austeros, “harsh, severe.”
words.note: Austere can also describe a stern, serious person: an austere headmaster.

mn.cue: AW, STARE at the bare walls
mn.text: Visitors to the old judge’s room can only say “Aw...” and stare: one stool, one candle, one plain table and nothing else. His room is {austere}.

scene.alt: An old man sits on a stool in a bare room with only a small table and a candle as a girl stares.

example

an ornate ceiling; an opulent hotel
after.cap: From praise to blame, and from fancy to bare.

after.html: Aesthetic (about beauty) sounds like ascetic (living a strict, self-denying life), but the two are unrelated. And austere is the opposite of ornate and opulent.

items.q: Choosing a paint color because it looks lovely is an ______ choice. Which word fits?
items.why: Aesthetic means having to do with beauty. Ascetic means self-denying.
Gaudy means tastelessly showy. Ornate and opulent can be praise; exquisite is praise.

items.q: Which word is the opposite of opulent?
items.why: Opulent means rich and luxurious; austere means plain and bare.
Flamboyant comes from French flamboyer, to blaze: a flamboyant person dresses and acts like a bright flame.
